extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and legal practitioners involved in patent litigation and prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the evidentiary standards and substantive criteria for (1) the sufficiency/enablement of patent specifications and (2) proof and evaluation of infringement and novelty in litigation. Focuses on the class of persons to whom a specification is addressed, admissibility and role of expert/artisan witnesses, and burdens of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of the specification (enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must express the mode of constructing, compounding, and using the invention 'in such full, clear, and exact terms, as to enable any person skilled in the art or science ... to make, construct, compound, and use the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The criterion is whether an ordinary workman of competent skill could execute an order from the specification and drawing, aided by general knowledge and reasonable mechanical means, without having to sit down and invent or 'tax his invention' to find out how to do it. If the workman must 'sit down and consider' and discover methods not stated, the specification is insufficient. (Examples: paddle-wheel angle case where required data such as stem lengths should have been given.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Class of persons to whom the specification is addressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Before determining sufficiency, ascertain the class of persons presumed to be addressed by the specification (e.g., workmen of a trade, practical chemists, competent engineers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard of sufficiency varies with the nature of the invention — machines for a particular use are presumed addressed to workmen who make similar machines; compositions to practical chemists; novel inventions depending on scientific principles may be addressed to engineers. Observe who will be likely to undertake to practice the invention to identify the proper addressee class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary skill limit (no extra inventive exertion required)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee must not frame a specification that requires those addressed to exercise more than the actual existing knowledge common to their trade or profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee may exhaust common knowledge but cannot require members of the trade to tax their ingenuity or exercise the inventive faculty to apply the directions. If the application requires solving a new problem or supplying something by inventive effort, the specification is bad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of scientific witnesses versus artisans
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific witnesses (persons thoroughly conversant with the science) and practical artisans serve different evidentiary functions; scientific witnesses may be satisfactory witnesses but cannot supply the invention missing from the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While a scientific person might, from a hint, invent the means and teach an artisan how to apply the specification, the specification should not be deemed sufficient merely because a scientist could, by fresh invention, enable the artisan. Evidence as to clearness and fulness may be given by scientific witnesses but sufficiency must be judged by the ability of competent practical workmen of ordinary skill (unless the invention is properly addressed to scientists/engineers).

rubrics_metrics.name: When invention is addressed to scientific persons
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention is entirely novel and depends on scientific principles not within the province of ordinary artisans, the specification may be presumed to be addressed to persons capable of applying those principles (e.g., engineers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases the specification ought to furnish the rules by which those persons could ascertain necessary parameters and the mechanical means to apply them. The required understanding is above manual mechanics and within ordinary skill of competent scientists/engineers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standard for proof of ability to apply specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The question is whether the witnesses satisfy that the specification gives the public the means of making a machine or product as claimed so that an ordinary workman of competent skill could execute an order by following the directions given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the jury believes a workman could not execute the order without inventing, then the specification is insufficient. The jury must assess credibility and whether testimony makes out the plaintiff's proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert evidence for identity/infringement — factual vs opinion distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of expert evidence: (1) testimony as to matters of fact (precise differences or resemblances observable by the senses) and (2) opinion whether those differences or resemblances are material to substantial identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The boundaries between fact and opinion can be shadowy; experts may point out differences and opine on materiality, but the ultimate legal question of identity is mixed law and fact and for the court (and jury) to decide. Experts must not be allowed to determine the issue for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court must instruct jury on legal significance of differences
rubrics_metrics.description: After differences/resemblances are ascertained, the court must instruct the jury what, in point of law, constitutes a difference or identity and whether a change amounts to a fresh invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court should not surrender this duty to expert witnesses. Experts can state opinions about materiality, but the question whether a change is legally a new invention or merely a mechanical equivalent is for the court to define.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and required foundation for expert conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert's positive testimony that two machines are 'in principle different' should show satisfactorily wherein the difference consists; bare assertion without explanation is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts should point out and explain specific points of resemblance or difference. Courts will not follow unsubstantiated expert conclusions; witness must tie opinions to observable facts or reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence required to establish prior existence (novelty defense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof that the thing patented existed before must be positive and credible; credible evidence of prior existence will outweigh negative evidence by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a credible witness's testimony of prior construction of an identical water-wheel counted as establishing lack of novelty. Mere testimony that a witness saw an article that 'might have been made' by a similar machine is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice requirement for prior user or prior publication defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: When a defendant relies on prior invention, knowledge, or use, he must give notice of the names and places of residence of persons he intends to prove had prior knowledge or use; for printed works, specify the particular part referred to if the work is general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural rule ensures plaintiffs can investigate and respond; failure to adequately notify can limit the admissibility or weight of the defense evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on evidence of superiority (improper relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence claiming to show the superiority of defendant's machine over the patentee's is improper except insofar as it tends to prove a substantial difference between the two devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superiority alone does not prove non-infringement; it is admissible only if it bears on whether the changes are substantial (i.e., amount to a different invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence of witnesses with interest (users, patentees, assignees, licensees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who have used the patented machine, patentees who have assigned rights, assignees for other districts, and licensees may be competent witnesses despite potential interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competency is not defeated by interest alone; evidence of motives or declarations of abandonment by an assignor after whole assignment may be inadmissible. Testimony by licensees or prior users is admissible but may carry limited weight depending on bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearsay and improper declarations as to prior user motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations of third parties as to their motives for prior use are inadmissible as mere hearsay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting to prove prior use by a third party, the defendant cannot rely on out-of-court statements of that third party about motives; direct evidence of use is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: When no recognized artisan class exists
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention is so entirely novel and depends on science rather than artisan practice, there may be no recognized class of artisans to whom the directions can be referred; the nature of the invention determines this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases the specification is presumed addressed to persons capable of applying the scientific principles, and sufficiency should be judged by their ability rather than manual artisans'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for statutory sale requirement by alien patentees
rubrics_metrics.description: When the defense alleges that an alien patentee failed to comply with statutory requirements (e.g., §13 of 1836 requiring sale to the public on reasonable terms), the burden of proof rests on the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a substantive allocation of burden in defenses alleging statutory noncompliance by the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud in obtaining patent extension must be directly litigated
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations of fraud in obtaining an extension of a patent can only be tried in a direct proceeding to impeach the patent and not collaterally in an infringement suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants in an infringement action may not use collateral attacks on extensions; a separate, direct proceeding is required to impeach the patent's validity on that ground.
